meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I'm so fast last night I cut the light switch and was in bed before the room was dark'?
meta.ogDescription: Quote Investigator traces this speed joke to 1917 — decades before Ali was born. He used it in 1974, but the viral wording matches no transcript.

answer.label: Said by Ali — but the joke wasn’t his
answer.sourceLine: Ali did tell this joke. The earliest instance Quote Investigator ↗ documents for him is a Village Voice dispatch from Ali’s training camp, 25 July 1974, where reporter Nick Browne transcribed it as “I’m so fast last night I cut the light and hit the switch and was in bed before the room was dark.” But the gag was already in print in April 1917 — long before Ali was born — and had passed through vaudeville, Abbott and Costello, and Satchel Paige before it reached him. The version circulating today is a garbled compression of Browne’s line.
answer.confidenceText: Ali really did use this gag — but he borrowed it, and this exact wording matches no documented transcript.

source.heading: The closest thing to a real source

docMeta.dd: Nick Browne, “The Rumble in the Jungle: Ali’s Camp: You Can’t Get Zaire From Here,” p. 9
The Marines Magazine, April 1917, p. 32 — Ali was born in 1942

source.excerpt: I’m so fast last night I cut the light and hit the switch and was in bed before the room was dark.
trail: April 1917 — the earliest known appearance. A Fort Mifflin correspondent writing as “Hablarias” in The Marines Magazine writes that a comrade “can switch off the lights and be back in bed before the room gets dark!” — recorded by Quote Investigator ↗.

1919 to 1945 — the gag goes professional. Moran and Mack use it at the Majestic (Chicago Tribune, 9 March 1919: “when I go to bed at night and turn out the light I’m in bed before the room is dark”), and an Abbott and Costello radio script picks it up in 1945, per the same chronology ↗.

1969 and 1971 — Satchel Paige attaches it to James “Cool Papa” Bell in the Washington Post (29 April 1969) and Jet (22 July 1971). Wikipedia ↗ notes the room in question had faulty wiring — a detail Paige tended to leave out.

1974 and 1975 — Ali’s turn. The Village Voice version of 25 July 1974 and a different New York Times version of 29 June 1975 are the only two Ali instances QI documents ↗. Neither matches the line that circulates today.
source.excerptNote: That is the sentence reporter Nick Browne transcribed in Ali’s camp. Note what the popular version does to it: “cut the light and hit the switch” collapses into “cut the light switch,” and a third, still more polished variant — “turned off the light switch in my hotel room” — has no documented source at all. Ali told it differently again in The New York Times of 29 June 1975: “I’m so fast I hit the light switch in my room and jump into bed before my room goes dark.” A joke retold from memory does not have one canonical wording, which is exactly why no version of this should be presented as a verbatim Ali quotation.

sourceLink.text: Quote Investigator: "When He Turned Out the Light He Was in Bed Before the Room Was Dark"

source.rightsHolder: The estate of Muhammad Ali (Muhammad Ali Enterprises, owned by Authentic Brands Group) and The Village Voice
source.rightsNote: The underlying joke — in its 1917 and 1919 forms — is long out of copyright. But the Ali wording is not. It reaches us through Nick Browne’s Village Voice article of 25 July 1974, a work first published well after 1931 and therefore still in copyright, and Ali’s own words and likeness are administered by Muhammad Ali Enterprises, acquired by Authentic Brands Group in November 2013 ↗ in partnership with the Ali family. The garbled version circulating online has no identifiable source at all, so no public-domain status can be claimed for it.

author.name: Muhammad Ali
author.heading: Muhammad Ali — borrower, not inventor
author.bio: Born Cassius Marcellus Clay Jr. in Louisville, Kentucky on 17 January 1942, Ali held the heavyweight crown across three decades and became, by the reckoning of his biographers ↗, as famous for his mouth as his left hand. He built the persona deliberately — he has said he took the idea from the wrestler “Gorgeous George” Wagner — freestyling rhymes, predicting knockout rounds, and working a repertoire of boasts before every fight. That repertoire was not all original. Like every great performer working a room, Ali picked up lines that landed, and the light-switch gag was one he inherited rather than invented.

cite.sourceCitation: Nick Browne, “The Rumble in the Jungle: Ali’s Camp: You Can’t Get Zaire From Here,” The Village Voice, 25 July 1974, p. 9 — the earliest Muhammad Ali instance documented by “Quote Origin: When He Turned Out the Light He Was in Bed Before the Room Was Dark,” Quote Investigator, 12 June 2013 (updated 17 February 2025). The joke itself is documented from The Marines Magazine, April 1917, p. 32.

misattribution.heading: What’s actually wrong here
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabricated quote — Ali really did tell this joke, and a reporter wrote it down. But two claims ride along with it that the record does not support: that Ali invented it, and that he said it in these words.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ documents the gag in The Marines Magazine of April 1917 — a Fort Mifflin correspondent writing as “Hablarias” jokes that a comrade “can switch off the lights and be back in bed before the room gets dark!” Ali was born in 1942. QI’s stated conclusion is that the line was in circulation by 1917 with no single originator identified.

items.who: “…I turned off the light switch in my hotel room and was in bed before the room was dark”
items.why: This is the version that dominates the internet — it appears on BrainyQuote ↗ with no date, publication or source of any kind. No period transcript records it. Barry Popik ↗ can only cite it to a modern tweet.

items.who: Moran and Mack, Abbott and Costello
items.why: The comedy team Moran and Mack were working it by 9 March 1919, per the Chicago Tribune, and a 1945 Abbott and Costello radio script has “I can turn off the lights and dive into bed before the room gets dark!” — both documented by QI ↗.

items.who: Satchel Paige, on James “Cool Papa” Bell
items.why: Paige used it in the Washington Post of 29 April 1969 (“Cool Papa was so fast he could get in bed before the room got dark”) and in Jet on 22 July 1971 — years before Ali. Wikipedia ↗ preserves the punchline Paige left out: the hotel room had a short in the switch.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: Ali said it, but he didn’t write it and he didn’t say it this way. Quote Investigator ↗ concludes the joke “was in circulation by 1917” and “has been adopted by a variety of comedians and athletes over the decades” — Ali being one of the last and loudest.

context.heading: Why a borrowed joke still sounds like Ali
lead: The Village Voice piece ran on 25 July 1974, months before Ali met George Foreman in Kinshasa on 30 October 1974 ↗. This was Ali in full pre-fight performance mode — the mode that made him one of the most quoted athletes who ever lived. A reporter in camp wrote down what he heard, and what he heard was a speed boast that had been making the rounds of barracks, vaudeville houses and dugouts for over half a century.

That is not a scandal; it is how comic material has always travelled. The gag works because the teller sells it, and Ali sold it better than the Marine correspondent who first put it in print in 1917. What is worth correcting is the modern habit of stamping a famous name on a line and calling the matter settled — which is precisely how the “hotel room” wording, sourced to nothing, became the version everybody repeats.
context.detailsSummary: The gag’s route to Ali, teller by teller
detailsBody: 1917 — A Fort Mifflin correspondent writing as “Hablarias” in The Marines Magazine gets the joke into print for the first time known.
1919 — The vaudeville team Moran and Mack are working it at the Majestic, per the Chicago Tribune of 9 March.
1945 — An Abbott and Costello radio script has the line “I can turn off the lights and dive into bed before the room gets dark!”
1969 and 1971 — Satchel Paige attaches it to his Negro Leagues teammate James “Cool Papa” Bell — the association most Americans still know it by.
1974 and 1975 — Ali takes it up, in two differently worded outings recorded by the Village Voice and The New York Times.
context.pull: Ali didn’t write the joke. He just gave it the best delivery it ever had.
